blocks.text: The concept of magnetic field

A magnet turns a compass needle and pulls iron filings without touching them, and so does a wire that carries a current. We describe this by saying that a magnet or a current sets up a **magnetic field** in the space around it, and that this field then acts on other magnets, currents and moving charges placed in it.

The idea is the same as for the electric field. Instead of one body acting on another directly across empty space, the source fills the surrounding space with a field, and the field at a point acts on whatever is placed at that point. The magnetic field is a **vector field**: at every point it has a magnitude and a direction, written $\vec{B}$.

The sources of a magnetic field are:
- moving charges and electric currents (a current in a wire, a beam of electrons in a tube);
- permanent magnets (whose field also comes, at the atomic level, from circulating and spinning electrons);
- a changing electric field (met later, in electromagnetic waves).

A charge at rest produces only an electric field; a moving charge produces both an electric and a magnetic field. In the same way, a magnetic field exerts a force only on a **moving** charge. A stationary charge, however strong the magnet near it, feels no magnetic force.

The magnetic field at a point is measured by the force it exerts on a test charge moving through that point. This force is perpendicular to both the velocity of the charge and the field, and it vanishes when the charge moves along the direction of the field.

$q$ = charge (C); $\vec{v}$ = velocity of the charge ($\text{m s}^{-1}$); $\vec{B}$ = magnetic field (T); $\theta$ = angle between $\vec{v}$ and $\vec{B}$. The force is largest, $qvB$, when the charge moves at right angles to the field and zero when it moves parallel or antiparallel to the field. This relation is used to define $\vec{B}$; the motion of charges in fields is studied in the lesson on Ampere's law.

The vector quantity whose magnitude at a point equals the force per unit charge per unit speed on a charge moving at right angles to the field there, $B = F/(qv)$, and whose direction is the direction in which the north pole of a small compass needle points at that point (a charge moving along this direction feels no force). It is also called magnetic flux density. SI unit: tesla (T).

The magnetic field is 1 tesla when a charge of 1 C moving with speed $1\,\text{m s}^{-1}$ at right angles to the field experiences a force of 1 N. Hence $1\,\text{T} = 1\,\text{N s C}^{-1}\,\text{m}^{-1} = 1\,\text{N A}^{-1}\,\text{m}^{-1}$, with dimensions $[\text{M}\,\text{T}^{-2}\,\text{A}^{-1}]$. A smaller non-SI unit, the gauss, is also used: $1\,\text{G} = 10^{-4}\,\text{T}$.

blocks.text:
**Magnetic field lines.** Just as electric field lines picture $\vec{E}$, magnetic field lines picture $\vec{B}$. They are drawn with these properties:
1. The tangent to a field line at any point gives the direction of $\vec{B}$ at that point.
2. Where the lines are closer together the field is stronger; where they spread out it is weaker.
3. Two field lines never cross, because the field cannot have two directions at the same point.
4. Magnetic field lines are **closed loops**. Outside a magnet they run from the north pole to the south pole and inside the magnet from south to north. Unlike electric field lines they do not start or end on 'charges', because isolated magnetic poles have never been found.
5. Around a long straight current-carrying wire they are concentric circles centred on the wire.

**Superposition.** If several currents or magnets are present, the field at a point is the vector sum of the fields they produce separately: $\vec{B} = \vec{B}_1 + \vec{B}_2 + \dots$ This principle is what lets us add up the contributions of tiny current elements in the Biot–Savart law.

Magnetic fields are produced by moving charges (currents) and act on moving charges (currents). A static charge neither produces a magnetic field nor experiences a magnetic force. $\vec{B}$ is a vector measured in tesla, $1\,\text{T} = 1\,\text{N A}^{-1}\text{m}^{-1} = 10^4\,\text{G}$.
Oersted's experiment

In 1820 the Danish physicist Hans Christian Oersted noticed during a lecture demonstration that a compass needle near a wire swung each time the current in the wire was switched on. His follow-up experiments gave the first clear evidence that electricity and magnetism are connected, and they launched the subject of **electromagnetism**.

**Arrangement.** A long straight wire is stretched horizontally in the north–south direction, a little above a freely pivoted compass needle and parallel to it. The wire is connected to a battery through a key and a rheostat.

**Observations.**
1. With the key open (no current) the needle rests along the wire, pointing north–south.
2. When current flows from south to north in the wire placed above the needle, the north pole of the needle is deflected towards the **west**.
3. When the current is reversed (north to south), the needle is deflected the other way, towards the east.
4. When the wire is placed below the needle instead of above it, the direction of deflection is reversed again.
5. The deflection grows when the current is increased or when the needle is brought closer to the wire. As soon as the current is switched off, the needle returns to the north–south direction.

**Conclusions.** A conductor carrying a current produces a magnetic field around it. The field exists only while the current flows, its direction depends on the direction of the current, and its strength increases with the current and decreases with distance from the wire. If a vertical wire carrying a current is passed through a horizontal card sprinkled with iron filings, the filings arrange themselves in concentric circles around the wire: the field lines of a long straight wire are circles in planes perpendicular to the wire, centred on it.

**Right-hand thumb rule (straight wire).** Imagine holding the wire in your right hand with the thumb pointing in the direction of the current. Your curled fingers then point in the direction of the magnetic field lines around the wire. Looking at the wire end-on, the field lines circulate anticlockwise when the current comes towards you and clockwise when the current goes away from you.

Apply it to observation 2: with the thumb pointing north along the wire, the fingers pass under the wire pointing west. The needle, which is below the wire, therefore feels a westward field and its north pole swings west. Above the wire the fingers point east, which is why placing the wire under the needle reverses the deflection.

The magnitude of the field of a long straight wire, $B = \mu_0 I/(2\pi r)$, is derived in the lesson on Ampere's circuital law. Here we need only its two features seen by Oersted: $B$ increases with $I$ and falls with distance $r$.

**Memory aid, SNOW:** current from **S**outh to **N**orth, wire **O**ver the needle, north pole deflects **W**est. Changing one of these (reversing the current, or putting the wire under the needle) makes the deflection east; changing both makes it west again.

The needle in Oersted's experiment usually does not turn through a full 90°. It settles along the resultant of the Earth's horizontal field (towards north) and the field of the current (towards east or west). Only when the current's field is much stronger than the Earth's field does the needle turn almost at right angles to the wire.
The Biot–Savart law

$dB$ = magnitude of the field at P due to the element (T); $I$ = current (A); $dl$ = length of the element (m); $r$ = distance from the element to P (m); $\theta$ = angle between $d\vec{l}$ and $\vec{r}$; $\mu_0$ = permeability of free space. In SI units $\mu_0/4\pi = 10^{-7}\,\text{T m A}^{-1}$.

Vector form. $\vec{r}$ points from the element to the field point; dividing by $r^3$ instead of $r^2$ allows for the length of $\vec{r}$ in the numerator, since $\vec{r}/r^3 = \hat{r}/r^2$. The cross product makes $d\vec{B}$ perpendicular to the plane containing $d\vec{l}$ and $\vec{r}$.

The constant that fixes the strength of magnetic fields produced by currents in vacuum: $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}\,\text{T m A}^{-1}$ (equivalently $\text{N A}^{-2}$ or $\text{H m}^{-1}$), so that $\mu_0/4\pi = 10^{-7}\,\text{T m A}^{-1}$. It plays the role for magnetism that $\varepsilon_0$ plays for electrostatics, and the two are linked by $c = 1/\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0} = 3\times10^{8}\,\text{m s}^{-1}$, the speed of light in vacuum.

**Direction of $d\vec{B}$.** $d\vec{B}$ is along $d\vec{l}\times\vec{r}$. Use the right-hand screw rule: turn a right-handed screw from $d\vec{l}$ towards $\vec{r}$ through the smaller angle; the direction in which the screw advances is the direction of $d\vec{B}$. In the figure, $d\vec{l}$ points to the right and $\vec{r}$ points up and to the right, so $d\vec{B}$ at P comes out of the page.

**Special cases.**
- $\theta = 0^\circ$ or $180^\circ$ (P lies on the line of the element, like point Q): $\sin\theta = 0$, so $dB = 0$. A current produces no field at points on its own line.
- $\theta = 90^\circ$ (P lies on the perpendicular through the element): $dB$ is maximum, $dB = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{I\,dl}{r^2}$.

**Field of a whole conductor.** An isolated current element cannot exist, because a steady current must flow round a closed circuit. The Biot–Savart law is therefore checked through its consequences: the field of a complete conductor is obtained by adding (integrating) the vector contributions of all its elements, $\vec{B} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi}\int \frac{d\vec{l}\times\vec{r}}{r^3}$, and these results agree with measurement.

blocks.text: **Common mistake:** $\theta$ in the Biot–Savart law is the angle between the current element $d\vec{l}$ and the line $\vec{r}$ joining the element to the point. It is not the angle between $\vec{r}$ and the perpendicular to the wire. Check: on the line of the element the field must come out zero.

blocks.problem: A short element of wire of length $\Delta l = 2\,\text{cm}$ lies at the origin along the $+x$ direction and carries a current of 5 A. Find the magnetic field it produces at the point $(0,\,0.4\,\text{m},\,0)$ on the $y$-axis.
blocks.solution:
Step 1: The point is on the $y$-axis, so $\vec{r}$ points along $+y$ and $r = 0.4\,\text{m}$. The element points along $+x$, so the angle between $d\vec{l}$ and $\vec{r}$ is $\theta = 90^\circ$ and $\sin\theta = 1$.

Step 2: Apply the Biot–Savart law: $dB = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{I\,\Delta l\,\sin\theta}{r^2} = 10^{-7}\times\frac{5\times0.02\times1}{(0.4)^2} = 10^{-7}\times\frac{0.1}{0.16} = 6.25\times10^{-8}\,\text{T}$.

Step 3: Direction: $d\vec{l}\times\vec{r}$ is along $\hat{i}\times\hat{j} = \hat{k}$, that is the $+z$ direction.

blocks.problem: A current element of length 2 mm carrying 5 A is placed at the origin pointing along $+y$. Find the magnitude and direction of the magnetic field at the point $(3\,\text{cm},\,4\,\text{cm},\,0)$.
blocks.solution:
Step 1: Find the distance from the element to the point: $r = \sqrt{(0.03)^2 + (0.04)^2} = 0.05\,\text{m}$.

Step 2: Find the angle between the element (along the $y$-axis) and the line joining it to the point. The $y$-component of $\vec{r}$ is 0.04 m, so $\cos\theta = 0.04/0.05 = 0.8$ and therefore $\sin\theta = 0.6$.

Step 3: Substitute in the Biot–Savart law, with the length converted to metres: $dB = 10^{-7}\times\frac{5\times(2\times10^{-3})\times0.6}{(0.05)^2} = 10^{-7}\times\frac{6\times10^{-3}}{2.5\times10^{-3}} = 2.4\times10^{-7}\,\text{T}$.

Step 4: Find the direction from the cross product $d\vec{l}\times\vec{r}$: $\hat{j}\times(0.03\,\hat{i} + 0.04\,\hat{j}) = 0.03\,(\hat{j}\times\hat{i}) = -0.03\,\hat{k}$. The part of $\vec{r}$ parallel to the element contributes nothing, and the field points along the negative $z$-axis.

blocks.text: Magnetic field on the axis of a circular current loop

The circular loop is the most important application of the Biot–Savart law: it is the basic unit of coils, galvanometers and solenoids, and it behaves like a tiny magnet.

**Set-up.** A circular loop of radius $R$ and centre O carries a steady current $I$. Its axis is the line through O perpendicular to the plane of the loop; take it as the $x$-axis. We want the field at a point P on the axis at distance $x$ from O.

**Step 1: field of one element.** Every element $d\vec{l}$ of the loop is at the same distance $r = \sqrt{x^2 + R^2}$ from P. The element is tangent to the loop, so it is perpendicular to the radius and to the axis, and therefore perpendicular to $\vec{r}$. With $\theta = 90^\circ$,
$$dB = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\,\frac{I\,dl}{x^2 + R^2}$$

**Step 2: direction and cancellation.** $d\vec{B}$ is perpendicular to $\vec{r}$, in the plane containing the axis and $\vec{r}$. Resolve it into a component $dB_x$ along the axis and a component $dB_\perp$ perpendicular to the axis. The element diametrically opposite, $d\vec{l}'$, produces a field $d\vec{B}'$ of the same size whose perpendicular component points the opposite way. Taking the elements in such pairs, all perpendicular components cancel and only the axial components survive.

**Step 3: axial component.** If $\theta$ is the angle between $d\vec{B}$ and the axis, the geometry of the figure gives $\cos\theta = R/\sqrt{x^2+R^2}$. So
$$dB_x = dB\cos\theta = \frac{\mu_0 I\,dl}{4\pi\,(x^2+R^2)}\cdot\frac{R}{(x^2+R^2)^{1/2}}$$

**Step 4: add round the loop.** Everything except $dl$ is the same for every element, and $\oint dl = 2\pi R$:
$$B = \frac{\mu_0 I R}{4\pi\,(x^2+R^2)^{3/2}}\times 2\pi R = \frac{\mu_0 I R^2}{2\,(x^2+R^2)^{3/2}}$$
For a tightly wound coil of $N$ turns the fields of the turns add, so $B$ is multiplied by $N$.
Field on the axis of a circular coil. $N$ = number of turns, $I$ = current (A), $R$ = radius (m), $x$ = distance of the point from the centre along the axis (m). The field is directed along the axis.
Put $x = 0$. This is the largest field anywhere on the axis. For a single turn, $B = \mu_0 I/2R$.

**How the field varies along the axis.** Dividing the two results, $\frac{B_{\text{axis}}}{B_{\text{centre}}} = \left(1 + \frac{x^2}{R^2}\right)^{-3/2}$. The field is greatest at the centre and falls symmetrically on both sides. At $x = R$ it is $1/(2\sqrt{2}) \approx 0.35$ of the centre value, and at $x = \sqrt{3}\,R$ it is exactly $1/8$ of the centre value.

**Far from the loop ($x \gg R$).** Neglecting $R^2$ beside $x^2$, $B \approx \frac{\mu_0 I R^2}{2x^3} = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\,\frac{2\,(I\pi R^2)}{x^3}$. The field falls as $1/x^3$, exactly like the axial field of a bar magnet with magnetic moment $m = I\pi R^2 = IA$. This is why a current loop is called a magnetic dipole, a result used in later lessons.

**Direction: right-hand thumb rule for a loop.** Curl the fingers of the right hand along the current in the loop; the outstretched thumb points along the field on the axis (and through the centre). Equivalently, the face of the loop at which the current appears **anticlockwise** to an observer behaves as a **north pole** (field lines come out of it), and the face at which the current appears **clockwise** behaves as a **south pole**. Note that on the axis the field has the same direction on both sides of the loop.

**Field lines of a loop.** Close to the wire the lines are nearly circles around the wire, as for a straight conductor. Near the centre they are almost straight and parallel to the axis, and all of them thread through the loop in the same direction before spreading out and closing round the outside, like the field of a short bar magnet.

blocks.problem: A circular coil of 100 turns and radius 8.0 cm carries a current of 0.40 A. Find the magnetic field (a) at its centre and (b) at a point on its axis 6.0 cm from the centre.
blocks.solution:
(a) At the centre: $B_0 = \frac{\mu_0 N I}{2R} = \frac{4\pi\times10^{-7}\times100\times0.40}{2\times0.08}$. Numerator: $4\pi\times10^{-7}\times40 = 5.027\times10^{-5}$. Dividing by 0.16 gives $B_0 = 3.14\times10^{-4}\,\text{T}$.

(b) On the axis: $R^2 + x^2 = 0.0064 + 0.0036 = 0.0100\,\text{m}^2$, so $(R^2+x^2)^{3/2} = (0.1)^3 = 1.0\times10^{-3}\,\text{m}^3$.
$B = \frac{\mu_0 N I R^2}{2(R^2+x^2)^{3/2}} = \frac{4\pi\times10^{-7}\times100\times0.40\times0.0064}{2\times1.0\times10^{-3}} = 4\pi\times10^{-7}\times128 = 1.61\times10^{-4}\,\text{T}$.

Check with the ratio formula: $(1 + x^2/R^2)^{3/2} = (1.5625)^{3/2} = 1.953$, and $3.14\times10^{-4}/1.953 = 1.61\times10^{-4}\,\text{T}$. Both fields point along the axis.

blocks.text: Field at the centre of a circular arc

Many exam questions use wires bent into arcs. The Biot–Savart law handles them directly. For an arc of radius $R$ that subtends an angle $\phi$ (in radians) at its centre, every element is at distance $R$ from the centre and perpendicular to the radius, so $\theta = 90^\circ$ for all elements and all the $d\vec{B}$ point the same way (perpendicular to the plane of the arc). Adding them, with total arc length $R\phi$:
$$B = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\,\frac{I\,(R\phi)}{R^2} = \frac{\mu_0 I\,\phi}{4\pi R}$$
For a full circle ($\phi = 2\pi$) this gives $\mu_0 I/2R$, as it must.

Straight wires whose lines pass through the centre (radial leads) contribute **nothing** at the centre, because for them $\theta = 0^\circ$ or $180^\circ$.

blocks.latex: B_{\text{arc}} = \frac{\mu_0 I\,\phi}{4\pi R}, \qquad B_{\text{semicircle}} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4R}, \qquad B_{\text{quarter}} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{8R}
blocks.text: $\phi$ = angle subtended by the arc at its centre, in radians; $R$ = radius of the arc (m). Direction from the right-hand thumb rule: clockwise current gives a field into the page at the centre, anticlockwise current gives a field out of the page.

blocks.problem: A closed loop is made of two semicircles of radii $a = 5\,\text{cm}$ and $b = 10\,\text{cm}$ with a common centre O, joined at their ends by two straight radial pieces (the shape is half of a flat ring). A current of 4 A flows anticlockwise along the outer semicircle and therefore clockwise along the inner one. Find the magnetic field at O.
blocks.solution:
Step 1: The straight pieces lie along lines through O, so $\theta = 0^\circ$ or $180^\circ$ for every element in them; they give no field at O.

Step 2: Inner semicircle (clockwise): $B_1 = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4a} = \frac{4\pi\times10^{-7}\times4}{4\times0.05} = 4\pi\times10^{-7}\times20 = 2.51\times10^{-5}\,\text{T}$, into the page.

Step 3: Outer semicircle (anticlockwise): $B_2 = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4b} = \frac{4\pi\times10^{-7}\times4}{4\times0.10} = 4\pi\times10^{-7}\times10 = 1.26\times10^{-5}\,\text{T}$, out of the page.

Step 4: The two fields are opposite, so $B = B_1 - B_2 = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4}\left(\frac{1}{a} - \frac{1}{b}\right) = 1.26\times10^{-5}\,\text{T}$, in the direction of the larger one, into the page.

blocks.text:
Revision points:
- Oersted (1820): a current produces a magnetic field; field lines of a straight wire are concentric circles; direction from the right-hand thumb rule.
- Biot–Savart law: $dB \propto I\,dl\sin\theta/r^2$, with $\mu_0/4\pi = 10^{-7}\,\text{T m A}^{-1}$; $d\vec{B}$ is perpendicular to both $d\vec{l}$ and $\vec{r}$.
- Circular loop: $B_{\text{centre}} = \mu_0 N I/2R$; on the axis $B = \mu_0 N I R^2/2(x^2+R^2)^{3/2}$; maximum at the centre; at large distance $B \propto 1/x^3$ like a dipole.
- Anticlockwise face of a loop is its north face; clockwise face is its south face.

**Exam tips and common mistakes.**
- Convert cm to m before substituting; $R$ in the denominator makes a factor-of-100 error easy.
- Do not forget the number of turns $N$, and remember that $B_{\text{centre}}$ has $2R$ (not $2\pi R$) in the denominator.
- If the same length of wire is rewound into $n$ turns, the radius becomes $1/n$ times, so $B_{\text{centre}} \propto n^2$.
- When a current divides between two arcs of a uniform ring, $I_1\phi_1 = I_2\phi_2$ (current is inversely proportional to arc length), so the two arc fields at the centre cancel exactly.
- Two loops in perpendicular planes with a common centre give fields at right angles: add them as vectors, $B = \sqrt{B_1^2 + B_2^2}$.

Because $\mu_0/4\pi = 10^{-7}$ exactly in the old definition of the ampere (and to better than one part in $10^9$ in the present SI), you can write $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7} \approx 1.257\times10^{-6}\,\text{T m A}^{-1}$ in every CUET calculation.

questions.stem: What was the main conclusion of Oersted's experiment with a current-carrying wire placed near a compass needle?
options: A magnet exerts a force on a stationary electric charge
An electric current produces a magnetic field around it
A changing magnetic field produces an electric current in a nearby circuit
Like magnetic poles repel each other and unlike poles attract
questions.explanation: Oersted observed that a compass needle placed near a wire is deflected only while current flows and that the deflection reverses when the current is reversed. This showed that an electric current sets up a magnetic field around the conductor, linking electricity with magnetism.

optionRationale.1: A stationary charge feels no magnetic force; Oersted's needle responded to a current, not a static charge.
optionRationale.3: Production of current by a changing magnetic field is electromagnetic induction, discovered later by Faraday.
optionRationale.4: This is a property of magnets known long before Oersted and is not what his experiment demonstrated.

questions.objective: State the conclusion of Oersted's experiment

questions.stem: A horizontal wire stretched in the north–south direction is placed just below a compass needle, and a current is passed through it from north to south. In which direction does the north pole of the needle deflect?
options: It stays along the north–south line
questions.explanation: Use the right-hand thumb rule. With the thumb pointing south along the wire, the fingers curl over the top of the wire pointing west. The needle is above the wire, so it feels a westward field and its north pole swings west. Two changes from the SNOW case (current reversed and wire under the needle) cancel out.

optionRationale.1: East would be correct if only one of the two conditions were reversed (for example north-to-south current with the wire above the needle).
optionRationale.2: The current's horizontal field is perpendicular to the wire, so the needle must turn away from the north–south line.
optionRationale.3: The field of the wire at the needle is horizontal (perpendicular to the wire and to the line joining wire and needle), so there is no vertical dip.

questions.objective: Apply the right-hand thumb rule to Oersted's arrangement

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): In Oersted's experiment, if the wire is shifted from just above the compass needle to just below it, keeping the current unchanged, the needle deflects in the opposite direction.
Reason (R): The magnetic field lines of a straight current-carrying wire are circles centred on the wire, so the field just below the wire is opposite in direction to the field just above it.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: The field lines around a straight wire are concentric circles. Going round a circle, the field direction at the top point is opposite to that at the bottom point. When the needle moves from below the wire to above it, the field it feels reverses, so the deflection reverses. R correctly explains A.

optionRationale.2: R is exactly the reason the deflection reverses, so it does explain A.
optionRationale.3: R is a correct description of the field of a straight wire.
optionRationale.4: A is an observed fact of Oersted's experiment.

questions.objective: Explain the reversal of deflection in Oersted's experiment using circular field lines

questions.stem: One tesla, the SI unit of magnetic field, is equivalent to which of the following?
questions.explanation: The defining relation of the field is $F = qvB$ for a charge moving at right angles to the field, so $B = F/(qv)$. Putting in units, one tesla is one newton per coulomb per metre per second, $1\,\text{N s C}^{-1}\text{m}^{-1}$. A coulomb per second is an ampere, so the tesla is the same as one newton per ampere per metre, $1\,\text{N A}^{-1}\text{m}^{-1}$.

optionRationale.1: The ampere must be in the denominator, because B = F/(IL) for a current-carrying wire.
optionRationale.2: N C⁻¹ is the unit of electric field, not magnetic field.
optionRationale.4: The factor $10^4$ relates tesla to gauss ($1\,\text{T} = 10^4\,\text{G}$); it does not belong in the SI equivalence.

questions.objective: Express the tesla in base and derived SI units

questions.stem: A small current element of length 1 cm lies at the origin along $+x$ and carries a current of 8 A. What is the magnetic field due to this element at the point $(0,\,0,\,0.2\,\text{m})$?
questions.explanation: The point lies on the $z$-axis, so the line joining the element to the point is perpendicular to the element and $\sin\theta = 1$. The magnitude is $dB = 10^{-7}\times\frac{8\times0.01}{(0.2)^2} = 10^{-7}\times\frac{0.08}{0.04} = 2\times10^{-7}\,\text{T}$. The direction follows the cross product of the element with the position vector, $\hat{i}\times\hat{k} = -\hat{j}$, so the field points along the negative $y$-axis.

optionRationale.1: Correct magnitude but wrong direction: $\hat{i}\times\hat{k} = -\hat{j}$, not $+\hat{j}$.
optionRationale.3: This results from dividing by $r$ instead of $r^2$.
optionRationale.4: This uses $\mu_0$ in place of $\mu_0/4\pi$, making the answer $4\pi$ times too large.

questions.objective: Use the vector form of the Biot–Savart law for magnitude and direction

questions.stem: At a point lying on the line of a current element (on $d\vec{l}$ extended), the magnetic field produced by that element is
options: zero, because the angle between $d\vec{l}$ and $\vec{r}$ is $0^\circ$ or $180^\circ$
maximum, because the point is nearest to the line of the current
questions.explanation: The Biot–Savart law gives $dB \propto \sin\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between the element and the line joining it to the point. On the line of the element, $\theta = 0^\circ$ or $180^\circ$, so $\sin\theta = 0$ and the element produces no field there.

optionRationale.2: The field is maximum for $\theta = 90^\circ$, on the perpendicular through the element, not on its line.
optionRationale.3: $d\vec{B}$ is always perpendicular to $d\vec{l}$, never along it; here it is zero anyway.
optionRationale.4: The field of an element varies as $1/r^2$ and is perpendicular to $\vec{r}$, never along it.

questions.objective: Identify points where a current element produces zero field

questions.stem:
Consider these statements about the magnetic field $d\vec{B}$ produced by a current element $I\,d\vec{l}$ at a point P whose position relative to the element is $\vec{r}$:
A. $dB$ varies inversely as $r^2$.
B. $d\vec{B}$ is directed along $\vec{r}$.
C. $d\vec{B}$ is perpendicular to both $d\vec{l}$ and $\vec{r}$.
D. $dB$ is maximum when $d\vec{l}$ is perpendicular to $\vec{r}$.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below.
questions.explanation: Write the law in vector form, $d\vec{B} = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{I\,d\vec{l}\times\vec{r}}{r^3}$. Its magnitude is $\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{I\,dl\sin\theta}{r^2}$, so the field falls as the inverse square of distance (A is true) and is largest when the angle is a right angle, where the sine equals one (D is true). Because the field comes from a cross product, it is perpendicular to both the element and the position vector, so C is true and B is false.

optionRationale.1: B is false; the field is radial only in Coulomb's law, not in the Biot–Savart law.
optionRationale.4: Leaves out A, which is true (inverse-square dependence).

questions.objective: Analyse the dependence and direction given by the Biot–Savart law

questions.stem: A circular coil of 40 turns and radius 5 cm carries a current of 1.5 A. What is the magnetic field at its centre? (Take $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}\,\text{T m A}^{-1}$.)
questions.explanation: Use the field at the centre of a coil of N turns and convert the radius to metres first (5 cm = 0.05 m): $B = \frac{\mu_0 N I}{2R} = \frac{4\pi\times10^{-7}\times40\times1.5}{2\times0.05} = 4\pi\times10^{-7}\times600 = 7.54\times10^{-4}\,\text{T}$. So the field is about $7.5\times10^{-4}\,\text{T}$, directed along the axis of the coil as given by the right-hand thumb rule.

optionRationale.2: This is half the correct value, as if $4R$ had been used in the denominator.
optionRationale.3: This is double the correct value, as if $R$ had been used instead of $2R$.
optionRationale.4: This ignores the number of turns (it is the field of a single turn).

questions.objective: Calculate the field at the centre of a circular coil

questions.stem: A circular loop of radius $R$ carries a steady current. At what distance from its centre, along its axis, does the magnetic field become one-eighth of its value at the centre?
questions.explanation: Dividing the axial-field formula by the centre-field formula gives the ratio $B_{\text{axis}}/B_{\text{centre}} = (1 + x^2/R^2)^{-3/2}$. Setting this ratio equal to one-eighth means $(1 + x^2/R^2)^{3/2} = 8$. Raising both sides to the power two-thirds gives $1 + x^2/R^2 = 4$, so $x^2 = 3R^2$ and the required distance is $x = \sqrt{3}\,R$ on either side of the centre.

optionRationale.1: At $x = R$ the ratio is $1/(2\sqrt{2}) \approx 0.35$, not $1/8$.
optionRationale.2: At $x = 2R$ the ratio is $5^{-3/2} \approx 0.089$, smaller than $1/8$.

questions.objective: Use the axial-field formula of a circular loop to locate a point

questions.stem: A uniform circular ring of wire has centre O and radius $R$. A current $I$ enters the ring at point A and leaves at point B through straight leads directed along the radii OA and OB extended, where angle AOB is $90^\circ$. What is the magnetic field at O?
questions.explanation: The radial leads give no field at O ($\theta = 0$). The current divides between the quarter arc (angle $\pi/2$) and the three-quarter arc ($3\pi/2$) in inverse ratio of their resistances, i.e. of their lengths: $I_1 = 3I/4$, $I_2 = I/4$. Fields: $B_1 = \frac{\mu_0 I_1(\pi/2)}{4\pi R} = \frac{3\mu_0 I}{32R}$ and $B_2 = \frac{\mu_0 I_2(3\pi/2)}{4\pi R} = \frac{3\mu_0 I}{32R}$. Both arcs carry current from A to B, one clockwise and one anticlockwise, so the fields are opposite and cancel.

optionRationale.1: This is the field of only one of the two arcs; the other arc gives an equal and opposite field.
optionRationale.3: This would be the field of the quarter arc if it carried the whole current $I$, which it does not.
optionRationale.4: This is the field of a semicircle carrying $I$, which does not describe this circuit.

questions.objective: Combine current division with the arc formula to find the field at a ring's centre

questions.stem: A given length of wire is first bent into a single circular turn and carries a current $I$. The same wire is then rewound into a circular coil of 2 turns and carries the same current. How does the magnetic field at the centre change?
questions.explanation: The length of wire is fixed, so $L = 2\pi R_1 = 2\times2\pi R_2$, which gives $R_2 = R_1/2$. For one turn $B_1 = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2R_1}$; for two turns $B_2 = \frac{\mu_0 (2) I}{2(R_1/2)} = 4\times\frac{\mu_0 I}{2R_1}$. Doubling the number of turns doubles the field, and halving the radius doubles it once more, so the field at the centre becomes four times as large.

optionRationale.2: This counts only the doubling of turns and forgets that the radius is halved.
optionRationale.3: The field depends on both $N$ and $R$; neither stays the same here.
optionRationale.4: Rewinding into more turns increases, not decreases, the field at the centre.

questions.objective: Show that B at the centre varies as N squared for a fixed length of wire

questions.stem: The figure shows the field $dB$ at point P on the axis of a circular loop due to the element $dl$ at the top of the loop. Which expression gives the component of $dB$ along the axis?
questions.explanation: In the figure the field $dB$ is drawn perpendicular to the line $r$. That line makes an angle $\alpha$ with the axis, where $\sin\alpha = R/\sqrt{R^2+x^2}$, so $dB$ itself makes an angle $90^\circ - \alpha$ with the axis. The axial component is therefore $dB\cos(90^\circ - \alpha) = dB\sin\alpha = dB\,R/\sqrt{R^2+x^2}$. Adding these components round the whole loop gives $B = \mu_0 I R^2/2(R^2+x^2)^{3/2}$.

optionRationale.1: This is the component perpendicular to the axis, which cancels in pairs.
optionRationale.2: This is the tangent of the angle, not a cosine or sine, and can exceed 1.
optionRationale.4: Only part of $dB$ lies along the axis; the perpendicular part cancels with that of the opposite element.

questions.objective: Resolve the field of a loop element into axial and perpendicular components

questions.stem: Match each situation in List-I with the magnitude of the magnetic field in List-II (single turn carrying current $I$, radius $R$).

left: A. Centre of a circular loop
B. Centre of a semicircular arc
C. Axis of a loop at a large distance $x$ ($x \gg R$)

questions.explanation: Full loop: $\mu_0 I/2R$ (A-II). A semicircle is half the loop, so half the field: $\mu_0 I/4R$ (B-III). On the axis far away, $(x^2+R^2)^{3/2} \approx x^3$, giving $\mu_0 I R^2/2x^3$ (C-I). The Biot–Savart law gives the element's field (D-IV).

optionRationale.1: Swaps the full loop and the semicircle; the full loop gives the larger field.
optionRationale.3: Swaps the far-axis field and the element field.
optionRationale.4: Puts the far-axis expression at the centre of the loop, where x = 0 would make it meaningless.

questions.objective: Recall field expressions derived from the Biot–Savart law

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): A current element produces no magnetic field at points lying on the line of the element.
Reason (R): According to the Biot–Savart law, the field of a current element is proportional to the cosine of the angle between $d\vec{l}$ and $\vec{r}$.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: The Biot–Savart law gives $dB \propto \sin\theta$, not $\cos\theta$. On the line of the element $\theta = 0^\circ$ or $180^\circ$ and $\sin\theta = 0$, so the field is zero and A is true. R is false: a cosine dependence would make the field maximum, not zero, on the line.

optionRationale.1: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
optionRationale.2: R is false, so 'both true' is wrong.
optionRationale.4: A is true; the field on the line of the element is zero.

questions.objective: Recognise the sine dependence in the Biot–Savart law

questions.stem: Which of the following is a genuine difference between the Biot–Savart law for a current element and Coulomb's law for a point charge?
options: Only the Coulomb field falls off as the inverse square of distance
Only the Biot–Savart field obeys the principle of superposition
The Biot–Savart field is along $\vec{r}$, while the Coulomb field is perpendicular to $\vec{r}$
The field of a current element depends on the angle between $d\vec{l}$ and $\vec{r}$, whereas the field of a point charge has no such angular dependence
questions.explanation: Both laws are inverse-square laws and both obey superposition. The Coulomb field of a point charge is radial and the same in every direction at a given distance. The field of a current element is perpendicular to $\vec{r}$ and varies as $\sin\theta$, being zero along the element's line.

optionRationale.2: Both electric and magnetic fields obey superposition.
optionRationale.3: The directions are reversed: the Coulomb field is along $\vec{r}$, the Biot–Savart field is perpendicular to it.

questions.objective: Compare the Biot–Savart law with Coulomb's law

questions.stem: A small positive charge is held at rest near the north pole of a strong bar magnet. What is the magnetic force on the charge?
options: It is directed towards the north pole
It is directed away from the north pole
It is perpendicular to the field lines at that point
questions.explanation: The magnetic force on a charge is $\vec{F} = q(\vec{v}\times\vec{B})$. For a charge at rest, $\vec{v} = 0$, so the force is zero no matter how strong the field is. Magnetic fields act only on moving charges and currents.

optionRationale.1: There is no magnetic attraction of a static charge; that would need $\vec{v} \ne 0$.
optionRationale.2: Repulsion along the field would make magnetism act like electrostatics, which it does not.
optionRationale.3: The force on a moving charge is perpendicular to B, but here the charge is not moving, so there is no force at all.

questions.objective: Recognise that a magnetic field exerts no force on a stationary charge

questions.stem: Two identical circular loops, each of radius $R$ and carrying current $I$, are placed with a common centre O, one in a horizontal plane and the other in a vertical plane. What is the magnitude of the resultant magnetic field at O?
questions.explanation: Each loop produces a field of magnitude $\mu_0 I/2R$ at the common centre, directed along its own axis. The horizontal loop has a vertical axis and the vertical loop has a horizontal axis, so the two fields are at right angles. Adding them by Pythagoras gives $B = \sqrt{2}\times\frac{\mu_0 I}{2R} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{\sqrt{2}\,R}$.

optionRationale.1: The fields would cancel only if the loops were coplanar with opposite currents.
optionRationale.2: This is the field of one loop alone.
optionRationale.4: This adds the two fields as if they were parallel; perpendicular vectors must be added by Pythagoras.

questions.objective: Add fields of loops in perpendicular planes as vectors

questions.stem: Two identical coaxial circular loops, each of radius 10 cm and carrying 2 A in the same sense, are placed 20 cm apart. What is the magnetic field at the point on the axis midway between them? (Take $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}\,\text{T m A}^{-1}$.)
questions.explanation: The midpoint lies on the common axis at a distance equal to the radius from each loop, $x = R = 0.1\,\text{m}$. Each loop alone gives $B_1 = \frac{\mu_0 I R^2}{2(2R^2)^{3/2}} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\sqrt{2}\,R} = \frac{4\pi\times10^{-7}\times2}{4\times1.414\times0.1} = 4.44\times10^{-6}\,\text{T}$. Because the currents circulate in the same sense, both fields point the same way along the axis and add: $B = 2B_1 = 8.9\times10^{-6}\,\text{T}$.

optionRationale.1: This is the field of only one loop.
optionRationale.3: This is $\mu_0 I/2R$, the field at the centre of one loop, not at a point on the axis at distance R.
optionRationale.4: The fields cancel only if the currents are in opposite senses.

questions.objective: Superpose axial fields of two coaxial loops
